extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in biology, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-level exposition of evolution (variation and selection) that prescribes how to define, measure, and test evolutionary hypotheses and distinguishes sources and modes of evolutionary change. Emphasises precise definitions, quantitative measurement, and proper empirical grounding of theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for quantitative exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism demands now quantitative exactness in these matters, and will henceforth not be content until it has obtained it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for numerical values and measures (e.g., 'What is the numerical value of the variability of which you speak? Have you a measure of this correlation? Did you test the magnitude of the inheritance of that character?'). Do not accept vague or purely verbal explanations; follow up definitions with quantitative measurement whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable to give to the terms 'evolution', 'selection', and other subsidiary terms definite and consistent meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating common words as having a single obvious meaning; supply precise definitions so that quantitative work and comparisons are possible. Re-phrase problems in operational terms when necessary (e.g., 'Can we describe the changes in organic phenomena by the same conceptual shorthand of motion as suffices to describe inorganic phenomena?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing before theorizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination solving the universe—propounding a formula before the facts which the formula is to describe have been collected and classified—is a wrong scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out necessary preliminary investigations and statistical inquiries before publishing theory (example: life-duration statistics and inheritance tests required before asserting selection-based theories). Crush speculative hypotheses by empirical tests ('Faraday's notion'—suppress untested fancy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require demonstration of quantitative validity for proposed evolutionary factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Any cause of progressive change in living forms is a factor of evolution; but before we can accept it as a factor we must not only have shown its plausibility, but if possible have demonstrated its quantitative validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each proposed factor (e.g., inheritance of acquired characters, genetic selection, bathmic tendencies) needs independent, careful numerical demonstration rather than rhetorical plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject invoking new causes without necessity (Occam's razor)
rubrics_metrics.description: To assume an 'inherent growth-force' producing the right variation at the right time and place is fundamentally unscientific; we propound a new cause when old ones have not been shown to be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler explanations tied to environment and selection unless quantitative evidence compels a new cause. Avoid postulating teleological or ill-defined bathmic forces without measured support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sources of change (a–d)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are the following sources of change in living forms possible: (a) change due to inherent tendencies in the individual or to bathmic influence; (b) change due to other individuals of the same living type (autogeneric); (c) change due to other living types (heterogeneric); (d) change due to physical environment (inorganic influence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which source(s) a hypothesis appeals to and treat each separately, providing measurements of their relative contributions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate modes of transmission: inheritance vs tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Progressive change must be handed on to the next generation materially by inheritance or mentally by the transmission of customs and institutions (tradition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a trait or social feature, determine whether it is inherited (biological) or traditional (cultural). Investigate cases where the distinction is doubtful (e.g., family habits) and measure how tradition and inheritance interact and affect stability of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise two fundamental processes establishing change
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in aggregate forms may be produced by (i) modifications of individual members not due to growth or age (acquired modification) and (ii) modifications due to death of some individuals or relatively greater fertility of others (selection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse evolutionary change as arising from acquired modification versus selection; each mode requires transmission (inheritance or tradition) to be permanent. Quantitatively test the effectiveness and permanence of each mode (e.g., numerical evidence for inheritance of acquired traits is 'yet wanting').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of selection (autogeneric, heterogeneric, inorganic, natural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection may be autogeneric (individuals struggle with same type), heterogeneric (with allied or different types), inorganic (physical environment), or a combination grouped as natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating selection's role, specify which kind is invoked and attempt to measure its effect independently; consider combined influences when describing natural selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require quantitative tests when applying biological theory to human societies
rubrics_metrics.description: More than one sociological work has obtained considerable reputation by applying the Darwinian theory without the least quantitative investigation to human societies; criticism demands quantitative exactness and will not be content until it has obtained it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept vague biological explanations for social phenomena; ask for measurable evidence before attributing social change to biological factors (cautionary example: sociological applications of Darwinian theory without numerical tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical language and vague conceptual shorthand in biology
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to the metaphysical character of the language of much of modern physics, metaphysics has found a foothold in biology; the problem ought to be expressed in words to operational effect rather than metaphysical shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace metaphysical or teleological wording with operational, testable statements. E.g., do not treat 'consciousness' or 'self-determination' as brief definers of life; rely on structural and measurable characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand specific quantitative measures for hypotheses about variation and inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: To writers who assert explanations in terms like 'relative variability of local races' or 'correlation of two organs' the reply should be: what is the numerical value of the variability? have you a measure of this correlation? did you test the magnitude of inheritance?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing causal explanations invoking variability, correlation, heredity, reversion, or telegony, always accompany claims with concrete statistical measures and tests; without these, such explanations are to be treated skeptically.
